key_terms.meaning: θ(t) = 2πf_c t + φ(t), in radians; the whole argument of the carrier cosine at time t, with f_c the carrier frequency in Hz
f_i(t) = (1/2π)·dθ/dt = f_c + k_f m(t), in Hz; the message moves the phase, and the slope of the phase is the frequency
Hz per volt; how many hertz the carrier shifts for each volt of message signal m(t)
β = Δf/f_m = k_f A_m/(2πf_m), dimensionless; peak deviation divided by modulating frequency
D = Δf_max/W, the largest deviation the system allows divided by the highest message frequency W
B_T ≈ 2(Δf + f_m) = 2f_m(β + 1), in Hz; a quick bandwidth estimate covering about 98% of the power
Amplitude of the n-th sideband pair in the FM spectrum; sidebands sit at f_c ± n f_m
β well below 1 (say under 0.3): carrier plus one sideband pair, bandwidth 2f_m, looks like AM
Reverse-biased junction whose capacitance falls as reverse voltage rises; the audio voltage across it pulls the oscillator frequency directly
Generate a small-index NBFM at a low crystal-controlled frequency, multiply frequency and deviation up, then heterodyne to the final carrier
A tuned circuit detuned from f_c turns frequency deviation into amplitude change, which an envelope detector then reads
Two tuned primary/secondary circuits feeding a balanced diode pair; output is an S-curve against frequency, zero at f_c
A balanced detector with a large storage capacitor across the diode load; its output follows the ratio of the two amplitudes, so amplitude noise is largely rejected without a limiter
(S/N)_o ÷ (C/N)_i, output signal-to-noise ratio divided by input carrier-to-noise ratio at the detector
Below a carrier-to-noise ratio of roughly 10 dB the FM output SNR falls steeply instead of linearly; the receiver goes quiet
The dB level by which a wanted co-channel signal must exceed an unwanted one before FM locks onto the wanted one only
Transmitter boosts high audio frequencies with a differentiator-like network before modulation; time constant 75 µs in most of the world, 50 µs in some countries
Receiver low-pass network that cuts the treble back to flat; it also cuts the high-frequency noise that pre-emphasis boosted
Unmodulated 19 kHz tone in FM stereo; the receiver doubles it to 38 kHz to lock its subcarrier oscillator
Sum of left and right occupies the baseband 0–15 kHz; the difference rides on a suppressed 38 kHz subcarrier

takeaways: In angle modulation the message moves the instantaneous phase, and the derivative of that phase is the instantaneous frequency, so FM is the integral of the message and PM is the message itself.
Narrowband FM carries one sideband pair and looks like AM, while wideband FM spreads power over many sidebands set by Bessel functions J_n(β).
Carson's rule B ≈ 2(Δf + f_m) is the bandwidth you must allocate in practice, and it grows in direct proportion to how much you widen the deviation.
Direct FM pulls an LC oscillator with a varactor; indirect FM builds a tiny deviation in a stable crystal oscillator and multiplies it up, which is why it holds the carrier frequency steady.
Every FM detector is a frequency-to-amplitude converter followed by an envelope detector; the balanced Foster–Seeley and ratio detector versions cancel the amplitude noise that comes along.
FM wins on figure of merit, but the prize is bought with bandwidth: the output SNR grows roughly as β³ while the bandwidth grows only as β.
FM behaves exactly as the formulas promise only above threshold, near 10 dB carrier-to-noise; below it the output collapses and the receiver goes quiet.
Pre-emphasis at the transmitter and de-emphasis at the receiver flatten the audio while pushing down the high-frequency noise that FM produces unevenly.
FM stereo keeps mono receivers working by putting L+R in the baseband, L−R on a suppressed 38 kHz subcarrier, and a 19 kHz pilot to keep the two synchronized.
bank_note: Long answers here are mostly derivations with block diagrams and curves — write the defining equations for FM and PM first, then draw the spectrum, the modulator or detector circuit, and finish with a noise or figure-of-merit comparison, quoting units at every number.

bank.q: Define instantaneous phase and instantaneous frequency of a sinusoid. Starting from v(t) = A cos[2πf_c t + φ(t)], show that in PM the instantaneous frequency is f_c + (k_p/2π)·dm/dt, and explain why FM needs an integrator before the phase modulator.
outline: Write v(t) = A cos θ(t) and define θ(t) as the instantaneous phase in radians
Differentiate θ(t) to get f_i(t) = (1/2π)dθ/dt
For PM, φ(t) = k_p m(t) with k_p in rad/V, so f_i = f_c + (k_p/2π)·m'(t)
For FM, φ(t) = 2πk_f ∫m dτ, so f_i = f_c + k_f m(t) with k_f in Hz/V
Conclude: PM follows the message slope, FM follows the message itself; FM from a phase modulator needs an integrator ahead of it

bank.q: Explain the spectrum of a sinusoidal-modulated FM signal using Bessel functions. Distinguish narrowband and wideband FM, and state and justify Carson's rule.
outline: Write v(t) = A Σ J_n(β) cos 2π(f_c + n f_m)t and identify the sideband pairs at f_c ± n f_m with amplitude A·J_n(β)
Note carrier amplitude becomes A·J_0(β), so carrier power can vanish at certain β
NBFM: β small, only J_0 and J_1 matter, bandwidth 2f_m, phasor picture like AM with a quadrature twist
WBFM: many sidebands, effective bandwidth about 2(Δf + f_m)
Carson's rule justification: sidebands fall off fast beyond n ≈ β + 1; total power in the FM wave stays A²/2 regardless of β

bank.q: Describe the direct and indirect methods of FM generation with block diagrams. Explain the role of the varactor in the direct method and of the frequency multiplier and mixer in the indirect method.
outline: Direct method: audio voltage across a reverse-biased varactor in the oscillator tank shifts the oscillator frequency
Problem with direct FM: carrier frequency stability depends on the LC oscillator, so an automatic frequency control loop is added
Indirect (Armstrong) method: crystal oscillator gives a stable carrier, a balanced modulator plus 90° phase shift produces NBFM with a very small β
Frequency multipliers raise both carrier and deviation by the same factor N
A mixer with a crystal local oscillator shifts the carrier to the assigned frequency without changing the deviation
Compare: direct FM gives large deviation in one step but poorer stability; indirect FM gives excellent stability but needs a long multiplier chain

bank.q: With a circuit diagram, explain the Foster–Seeley discriminator and its S-curve. How does a slope detector differ from it?
outline: Slope detector: a tuned circuit off-resonance converts frequency change into amplitude change, then an envelope detector; it is simple but nonlinear and sensitive to AM
Foster–Seeley: primary tuned to f_c, secondary tuned to f_c with a centre tap; two diodes see voltages that add on one side and subtract on the other
Output is the difference of the two diode voltages, giving an S-shaped curve with zero output at f_c
Linearity holds only over the straight part of the S-curve, typically a small fraction of f_c
Needs an amplitude limiter ahead of it because the output also responds to amplitude changes; explain why the balanced connection cancels common AM

bank.q: Explain pre-emphasis and de-emphasis with circuit diagrams, frequency-response curves and typical time constants. Why does FM noise rise with frequency?
outline: FM discriminator output noise power density rises with frequency squared, so treble is far noisier than bass
Pre-emphasis: a high-pass RC network at the transmitter boosts highs above a corner frequency f_1 = 1/(2πτ)
De-emphasis: a low-pass RC network at the receiver with the same τ restores a flat audio response
Typical τ = 75 µs (f_1 ≈ 2.1 kHz), 50 µs in some countries
Net effect: audio unchanged, high-frequency noise reduced; state the improvement in output SNR as an integral of the noise weighting

bank.q: Explain FM stereo multiplexing with block diagrams of the transmitter and the receiver. What is the role of the 19 kHz pilot?
outline: Left and right audio are matrixed into L+R (0–15 kHz) and L−R
L−R amplitude-modulates a suppressed 38 kHz subcarrier (DSB-SC)
The composite baseband is L+R, the 38 kHz DSB-SC difference, and a 19 kHz pilot tone added at low level
The pilot is exactly half the subcarrier frequency so the receiver can double it in a locked oscillator and recover the 38 kHz carrier coherently
Receiver: FM discriminator → de-emphasis and 0–15 kHz low-pass for L+R → 19 kHz pick-up, doubler, synchronous detector for L−R → adder and subtractor give L and R
A mono receiver ignores everything above 15 kHz and plays L+R, so the service is compatible

bank.q: An FM wave is v(t) = 10 cos(2π × 10⁷ t + 4 sin 2π × 2000 t) volts across a 50 Ω load. Find the carrier frequency, peak frequency deviation, modulation index, bandwidth by Carson's rule, and the average power delivered.
outline: Compare with A cos(2πf_c t + β sin 2πf_m t): f_c = 10 MHz, β = 4, f_m = 2 kHz
Peak deviation Δf = β f_m = 4 × 2000 = 8 kHz
Bandwidth B_T ≈ 2(Δf + f_m) = 2(8 + 2) kHz = 20 kHz
Power P = A²/(2R) = 100/(2 × 50) = 1 W, independent of β
Mention that sidebands lie at 10 MHz ± n × 2 kHz with amplitudes 10 J_n(4) volts

bank.q: An Armstrong transmitter starts with a crystal oscillator at 1 MHz and an NBFM modulator that gives a peak deviation of 200 Hz. Design the multiplier chain and the final mixer needed to reach a carrier of 100 MHz with 75 kHz deviation.
outline: Required multiplication N = 75 000/200 = 375
Carrier after multiplication = 1 MHz × 375 = 375 MHz
Choose a practical chain, for example ×3, ×5, ×5, ×5, giving 375
Heterodyne down with a 275 MHz local oscillator to land at 100 MHz
Deviation is unchanged by the mixer: 75 kHz at 100 MHz
Note that the mixer must not introduce large deviation error, so a crystal local oscillator is used

bank.q: An AM receiver with envelope detection and 100% modulation is compared with an FM receiver having β = 5. Using figure of merit 2/3 for AM and (3/2)β²(β + 1) for high-index FM, find the improvement in dB, and compare the bandwidths if the message occupies 15 kHz.
outline: AM figure of merit = m²/(2 + m²) = 1/3 for m = 1, expressed as 2/3 depending on the reference point chosen — state the definition used
FM figure of merit = (3/2)(25)(6) = 225
Ratio = 225/(2/3) ≈ 338, that is about 25 dB improvement
AM bandwidth = 2 × 15 = 30 kHz; FM bandwidth ≈ 2(75 + 15) = 180 kHz
Conclude that FM pays roughly six times the bandwidth for about 25 dB better output SNR

bank.q: A de-emphasis network uses R = 10 kΩ and C = 0.0075 µF. Find its time constant and 3 dB corner frequency, and state what value of pre-emphasis time constant must be used at the transmitter.
outline: The transmitter pre-emphasis network must have the same τ = 75 µs so the two responses cancel
Above f_1 the pre-emphasis network gives about +6 dB per octave and the de-emphasis gives −6 dB per octave
The noise that rides on the treble is attenuated at the receiver without touching the audio

bank.q: Derive the figure of merit of an FM receiver with a sinusoidal message and compare it with AM. Explain why FM trades bandwidth for noise performance, and state the limit of this trade.
outline: Set up the detector input as carrier plus narrowband noise, resolved into in-phase and quadrature components
The quadrature noise produces an output noise power density that rises as f² across the baseband
Integrate over the baseband to get output noise, and write output signal power from the deviation
Obtain FOM = (3/2)β²(β + 1) for high index, against 1/3 (or 2/3) for AM with m = 1
Bandwidth grows as β while SNR grows as β³ — the cubic law
The trade stops at threshold; below about 10 dB carrier-to-noise the linear analysis fails

bank.q: Explain the threshold effect in FM. Define threshold and capture ratio, and describe two methods of extending the threshold.
outline: Define threshold as the carrier-to-noise ratio at which output SNR begins to fall steeply, typically around 10 dB for conventional FM
Cause: noise spikes take the resultant phasor around the origin, giving full-scale clicks at the detector output
Sketch the output SNR against input CNR curve, showing the linear part and the sharp knee
Capture ratio: the wanted signal must exceed a co-channel interferer by a few dB before the discriminator follows only the wanted one — this is why co-channel FM interference is tolerable
Threshold extension: FM feedback (FMFB) receiver narrows the IF bandwidth to follow the instantaneous frequency; phase-locked loop detector tracks the carrier and ignores clicks
State the cost: added complexity and possible loss of deviation range

bank.q: An FM broadcast service is to be planned for a city. Using the ideas of deviation, Carson bandwidth, detector choice, pre-emphasis and stereo multiplexing, justify the choice of each block in the transmitter and receiver chain and state which blocks decide the final audio quality.
outline: Transmitter: stable carrier from a crystal and multiplier chain or a direct varactor oscillator with AFC; deviation set to the standard maximum
Carson's rule fixes the channel width; guard bands between channels follow
Pre-emphasis network before the modulator with τ = 75 µs
Stereo coder: L+R, L−R on suppressed 38 kHz subcarrier, 19 kHz pilot
Receiver: RF amplifier, mixer to a fixed IF, limiters to remove AM, discriminator (ratio detector or balanced detector)
De-emphasis and stereo decoder after the discriminator; low-pass filter for the audio
Quality decided by IF bandwidth, limiter gain, deviation used and the de-emphasis/pre-emphasis match; evaluate the cost of wider deviation versus adjacent-channel interference

glossary.def: Any modulation in which the message changes the phase angle of the carrier rather than its amplitude; FM and PM are its two forms.
Modulation in which the instantaneous frequency of the carrier is f_c + k_f m(t), so the phase carries the integral of the message.
Modulation in which the instantaneous phase is shifted in proportion to the message, so the frequency deviation follows the derivative of the message.
The rate at which the phase of the carrier advances, f_i = (1/2π)dθ/dt, in hertz.
The peak amount by which the carrier frequency moves away from f_c, in hertz.
The ratio Δf/f_m, dimensionless; it decides how many sidebands carry significant power.
FM with β much less than 1, whose spectrum is a carrier and one sideband pair inside 2f_m.
FM with β of order 1 or more, whose spectrum spreads over many sideband pairs.
The practical bandwidth estimate B ≈ 2(Δf + f_m) hertz for an FM signal.
The function J_n(β) that gives the amplitude of the n-th sideband pair in a sinusoidally modulated FM wave.
A reverse-biased diode used as a voltage-controlled capacitor, the usual tuning element in direct FM modulators.
The indirect FM scheme: make a small-index NBFM at a stable low frequency, multiply, then mix to the final carrier.
A circuit that converts frequency deviation into a proportional voltage; the heart of an FM demodulator.
A balanced tuned-transformer diode detector whose output is an S-curve of voltage against frequency, zero at f_c.
A balanced FM detector that responds to the ratio of two tuned-circuit voltages, so it rejects amplitude noise without a separate limiter.
A hard-clipping IF stage that strips amplitude variations from the FM wave before the discriminator.
The ratio of output signal-to-noise ratio to input carrier-to-noise ratio of a receiver, used to compare modulation schemes.
The sudden fall in FM output signal-to-noise ratio once the carrier-to-noise ratio drops to roughly 10 dB.
The level difference in dB by which a wanted FM signal must exceed a co-channel unwanted one before it captures the receiver.
Boosting of high audio frequencies at the FM transmitter to equalise the rising noise spectrum at the receiver.
The matching high-frequency cut at the FM receiver that restores flat audio and removes the boosted noise.
The unmodulated 19 kHz signal in FM stereo that synchronises the receiver's 38 kHz subcarrier generator.
A carrier placed above the audio baseband to carry extra information, such as the L−R stereo difference at 38 kHz.
The composite baseband of L+R, the DSB-SC L−R on 38 kHz, and the 19 kHz pilot, all sent on one FM carrier.
